{{Short description|American mathematician (born 1963)}}
{{Use dmy dates|cs1-dates=ly|date=February 2022}}
{{Use list-defined references|date=February 2022}}
'''Eve Alexandra Littig Torrence''' (born 1963){{r|lc}} is an American mathematician, a [[professor emerita]] of mathematics at [[Randolph–Macon College]],{{r|em}} and a former president of mathematics society [[Pi Mu Epsilon]]. She is known for her award-winning writing and books in mathematics, for her [[Mathematics of paper folding|mathematical origami]] art,{{r|ex}} and for her efforts debunking overly broad claims regarding the ubiquity of the [[golden ratio]].{{r|gr|wp}}

==Education, career, and service==
Torrence was an undergraduate at [[Tufts University]].{{r|em|ex}} She completed her Ph.D. in 1991 at the [[University of Virginia]]; her dissertation, ''The Coordination of a Hexagonal-Barbilian Plane by a Quadratic Jordan Algebra'', was supervised by John Faulkner.{{r|mg|uv}}

She was Claire Booth Luce assistant professor at [[Trinity Washington University]] from 1991 to 1994,{{r|te}} before joining the Randolph–Macon College faculty in 1994.{{r|ex}} She earned tenure there in 1999, and became a full professor in 2008.{{r|bu}} She retired in 2021,{{r|bu|3p}} and was given the Bruce M. Unger Award by Randolph–Macon College on the occasion of her retirement.{{r|bu}}

She served as president of [[Pi Mu Epsilon]], the US national honor society in mathematics, from 2011 to 2014.{{r|ex}} The Maryland-District of Columbia-Virginia Section of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] gave her their Sister Helen Christensen Service Award in 2019.{{r|hc}}

==Selected works==
Torrence won the 2007 Trevor Evans Award of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] for a paper she wrote with Adrian Rice on [[Dodgson condensation]]:{{r|te}}

 | last1 = Torrence | first1 = Bruce F.

 | publisher = Cambridge University Press
 | title = The Student's Introduction to Mathematica: A Handbook for Precalculus, Calculus, and Linear Algebra
 | year = 1999}}{{r|si}}
*{{citation
 | last = Torrence | first = Eve
 | publisher = Dover Publications
 | title = Cut and Assemble Icosahedra: Twelve Models in White and Color
 | year = 2011}}

A sculpture, "Sunshine", by Torrence is displayed in a Randolph–Macon College building lobby; it depicts the [[compound of five tetrahedra]] as five interlocked aluminum shapes, inspired by an origami version of the same compound folded by [[Tom Hull (mathematician)|Tom Hull]].{{r|3p}} She also won the "Best in Show" award in a 2015 juried mathematical art exhibit, for her pieces titled "Day" and "Night", mathematical origami using folded cardstock [[rhombus|rhombi]] to make [[hyperbolic paraboloid]] surfaces, connected in the pattern of a [[rhombic dodecahedron]]:{{r|ex}}
